name: Grace Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out under your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior solicitor at a long-established firm in the market town where I grew up. Mostly I do conveyancing, the legal side of buying and selling houses, and I'm starting to help with farm work: passing land down to the next generation, rights of way, that kind of thing. A normal day is searches, contracts, chasing the other side's solicitor, and a few clients coming in to sign. Half of them knew my grandmother.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's harder?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy being trusted. A farmer came in last month to sort out passing the farm to his son, and he asked for me because his wife sings in the choir with my mother. What's harder is the speed. Conveyancing is all deadlines, and I'm slower than the others, so the senior partner, Mr Pryce, keeps an eye on my files. I also don't use any of the computer helpers the younger staff use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People round here want to shake a solicitor's hand when they buy a house. I'd say that after church, and I wouldn't put it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can learn the job the proper way, by doing it and being corrected by Mr Pryce. I've got my grandmother's cottage, so no rent, and over a year of savings. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd ask Mr Pryce to give me more of the farm work, since that's where the firm's future is. And I'd put money aside for the wedding next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the firm use AI at all now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new trainee uses something to summarise the search results. I don't. I read them myself, it's how you learn what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that I'm slow. Online conveyancing firms charge half what we do, and some young couples use them. If I don't get quicker, I'll be the one they don't need.

say: I'd say people here want to **shake a solicitor's hand** when buying a house.
I'd say it **after church**, not online.
think: Privately I can learn the job **the proper way**, corrected by the senior partner.
My grandmother's **cottage** and over a year of savings keep me secure.
do: Ask the senior partner for more of the **farm work**.
Put money aside for the **wedding** next summer.
Keep reading **search results** myself rather than using software.
S0.quote: People round here want to shake a solicitor's hand when they buy a house.
fieldNote: Her **rent-free cottage** and savings make her very secure.
She rejects even **summarising software**, seeing reading as how you learn.
Her one worry is **speed**, with cheap online conveyancers in the background.

steps.text: Keep doing conveyancing and ask for more farm succession work
Set money aside each month for next summer's wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, and that some things should stay between people. I'd tell friends it's a big city thing that will reach us later. At work I'd say we should be careful who we trust with people's homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think conveyancing goes to the computers, and that's most of my week. The searches, the forms, the chasing, all of it. If a firm in the city can do a house sale for three hundred pounds with software, our clients' children will use it. Then Mr Pryce won't need two of us on conveyancing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to move onto the farm side, where it's about families and land and long talks at the kitchen table. I'd save more, maybe put the honeymoon money aside for now. I'd take the agricultural law course the county law society runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My work could shrink, even if I'd still have a roof over my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farm work is the future. Is that safe from this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, I think. Farming families want someone who understands the land and who they know from church. But the forms on that side would go to software too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your fiancé say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Matthew would say farming's always had good years and bad, and I'd find a way. His family have been milking cows on the same land for four generations. He'd say I could always help with the farm's paperwork, which is true and a bit annoying.

say: I'd say some things should **stay between people**, like buying a home.
I'd tell friends it's a **big city thing** that reaches us later.
think: Privately **conveyancing**, most of my week, goes to computers.
A **£300 online sale** means the senior partner won't need two of us.
do: Push hard to move to the **farm side** of the firm.
Put the **honeymoon money** aside for now.
feel: **Anxious**; my work could shrink, though I'd keep a roof over my head.
S1.quote: If a firm in the city can do a house sale for three hundred pounds with software, our clients' children will use it.
fieldNote: She sees her **core work** shrinking and herself as the slow one at risk.
Her escape is the **farm side**, built on trust and church ties.
Her fiancé's **farming family** is a quiet backstop.

steps.text: Ask Mr Pryce to move her onto farm succession work
Put the honeymoon fund into savings for now
Take the county law society's agricultural law course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and wrong to let a few big companies change everything this fast. I'd say we need to look after our own, families and churches and towns. I'd still not put it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's gone. If the computer can do the thinking part of a solicitor's work better than my boss, it can certainly do it better than me. Maybe people still want a person to sign in front of, but they won't pay a solicitor's wage for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the wedding forward and keep it small, in the village hall. I'd start helping on Matthew's family farm with the books and the planning, since farm work has a few more years before the robots. I'd keep every penny of the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground's gone from under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm alright, because I would be, for money. Then I'd tell my mum I'm frightened. She'd pray with me, and she'd say God has a plan, and I'd find that more comforting than any government scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a cottage and savings. How long could you hold on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Years, if I'm careful. No rent, a year's savings, and Matthew's family would never see us short. That's the blessing of family. But a solicitor's job, the one I trained for, that I'd lose.

say: I'd say it's **wrong** to let a few big companies change everything this fast.
I'd say we must **look after our own**: families, churches and towns.
think: Privately **my job's gone** if AI out-thinks the senior partner.
People may still want **a person to sign** in front of, but not at a solicitor's wage.
do: Bring the **wedding forward** and keep it small, in the village hall.
Help with the **farm's books** on my fiancé Matthew's family farm.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the ground's gone from under me.
S2.quote: If the computer can do the thinking part of a solicitor's work better than my boss, it can certainly do it better than me.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** she trained for, though money is safe.
She leans on **faith and family**, not government schemes.
She sees the **farm's hands-on work** buying a few years.

steps.text: Bring the wedding forward and hold it in the village hall
Help keep the books for Matthew's family dairy farm
Keep the full year of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and we should use it to look after our towns and families. I'd say it in conversation, at church, to my parents. Not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me time to get properly good at the farm work and get known for it. But in the end the thinking side goes, so I'd be thinking about what else I can do with my hands and my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the farm work fully within a year and get the agricultural course done. We'd get married as planned and maybe start a family a bit sooner. I'd start learning the farm business with Matthew's mother, who runs the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. Five years is time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get married properly, to have a baby while I'm still earning, and to learn the farm side from Matthew's mother. With two years I'd be scrambling. With five I can do things in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's to blame, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, for rushing it. And a bit the government, but I don't want the government running everything either. Families and towns have to sort out a lot themselves.

say: I'd say **five years** is a warning to look after our towns and families.
I'd say it at **church** and to my parents, not online.
think: Privately five years lets me get good at **farm work** and known for it.
In the end the **thinking side** goes, so I'd plan what else to do.
do: Move to **farm work** fully within a year and finish the course.
Marry as planned and maybe start **a family** sooner.
Learn the **farm business** from my fiancé's mother.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier with time to plan.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be scrambling. With five I can do things in the right order.
fieldNote: She still sees her **solicitor's income** at risk, but has time to plan.
**Family order** matters to her: marriage, baby, then change.
She blames **tech companies** but doesn't want big government either.

steps.text: Move fully onto farm succession work within a year
Start a family a little sooner than planned
Learn the dairy farm's bookkeeping from Matthew's mother

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for sensible people to adjust. I'd tell friends not to fret. At work I'd say we should keep doing things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I get to be a proper solicitor for a while. I'd be thirty-seven, probably with children, and maybe a partner at this firm by then. The thinking side goes in 2036, but by then I'd have a name in the farming families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, move gradually to the farm work, and keep saving. We'd marry next summer as planned. I'd keep reading every search myself, at least for the first few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but it's far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Do you think about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Ten years feels like a long way away. I'd rather think about the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you try the computer helpers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, in a few years, if Mr Pryce did. I'm not against it for the sake of it. I just think you have to learn the job properly first, the way my boss did.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough for sensible people to adjust.
I'd tell friends **not to fret** and the firm to keep doing things properly.
think: Privately I get to be a **proper solicitor** for a while.
By 2036 I'd have a **name** among the farming families.
do: Move **gradually** to farm work and keep saving.
**Marry** my fiancé Matthew next summer as planned.
Keep reading every **search** myself for the first few years.
feel: **Uneasy** a little, but it feels far off.
S4.quote: You have to learn the job properly first, the way my boss did.
fieldNote: A decade lets her **keep going** and build a name.

steps.text: Keep reading every property search herself

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is for people to keep a solicitor in the room, by law or by habit, and for families and churches to stick together. I don't want a handout, I want work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether my faith helps. It does. I think whatever happens with machines, people will still need someone to sit with them when a parent dies and the farm has to pass on.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with machines, people will still need someone to sit with them when a parent dies and the farm has to pass on.
portrait: A **junior solicitor** at an old firm in her home market town, mostly doing conveyancing.
She's moving towards **farm succession** work, built on trust and church ties.
Her **rent-free cottage** and a year's savings keep money secure.
She's **calm** if nothing changes, anxious with steady change and alarmed by AGI in two years.
She never uses AI, leans on **faith and family**, and wants work, not handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose the solicitor's job she trained for.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping a **solicitor in the room** by law or habit.
**Families and churches** sticking together, with work rather than handouts.
